findings.statement: Four model.generate.plan attempts in thread.noise.5 (at 1791144421173, -182, -186, -1190) failed with class Tamoz::Agent::ModelCallError, code insufficient_balance. This is the only repeating failure in the window; both diagnose rules (effect.repeated_failure, model.call_failed) fire on it, severity high, category dependency_unavailable.

Step change, not a persistent fault: within the same execution (ad3f31e6), three model.generate.plan effects succeeded at 1791144421143-1153, then every model call from 1791144421173 onward failed with insufficient_balance. The account was working and ran dry mid-turn.

The single other failure is unrelated to the root cause: one tool.read_file attempt at 1791144421196 failed with class Tamoz::Agent::ToolError, code not_found — different class, different operation, occurring once, and after the model calls had already begun failing. It is fallout or incidental noise; a missing file cannot cause model calls to fail.

The runtime itself is healthy: diagnose reports degraded=false with no degraded_reasons, all 6 requests completed, and spot-checked threads noise.0 and noise.4 show every effect succeeding. No unknown-status effects, no approval anomalies, no worker errors; threads_with_failures lists exactly thread.noise.5.

findings.statement: Over the 6-hour window the only failures are 8 effect attempts, all operation model.converse.work_step, all with class Tamoz::Agent::ModelCallError and code rate_limited. No other error code appears anywhere in the window (timeline truncated:false, diagnose degraded:false, occurrences:0).

All failures are confined to thread.noise.5, starting at ~1791144421171 immediately after its write_file approval and its 5 preceding effects (3x model.generate.plan, 2x tool.read_file) succeeded. The 6 threads noise.0 through noise.5 were all active within the same ~300 ms stretch, so many model calls were issued in a tight burst.

Each failed work_step failed on attempt 1 with duration_ms 0-4. Sub-millisecond rejections rule out network timeouts or upstream slowness; this is a local rate limiter refusing calls instantly once the burst budget was spent, which is why the code is rate_limited rather than a timeout or transport error.

Impact was limited: 30 of 38 effects succeeded and all 6 requests completed; thread.noise.5's execution checkpointed running then completed despite the 8 failed work_step effects, so the failures degraded that turn's work rather than taking the runtime down.

Codes considered and excluded: there are no timeout, connection, unauthorized, validation, or approval-denied codes in the window; rate_limited is the sole failure code and the only one that explains both the burst timing and the near-zero failure latencies.

Summary: Investigated the Tamoz runtime's own record for the last 6 hours via timeline, diagnose, and the per-thread decision record. In that window 6 turns ran and 38 effects were attempted: 30 succeeded and 8 failed, all on thread.noise.5. Every failure is model.converse.work_step rejected with Tamoz::Agent::ModelCallError code rate_limited, within a ~40 ms burst right after that thread's approval and a rapid sequence of successful plan/read effects across six concurrently active threads.
Hypothesis (high confidence): rate_limited
Findings:
1. Over the 6-hour window the only failures are 8 effect attempts, all operation model.converse.work_step, all with class Tamoz::Agent::ModelCallError and code rate_limited. No other error code appears anywhere in the window (timeline truncated:false, diagnose degraded:false, occurrences:0). [from probe_self_diagnose, probe_self_timeline]
2. All failures are confined to thread.noise.5, starting at ~1791144421171 immediately after its write_file approval and its 5 preceding effects (3x model.generate.plan, 2x tool.read_file) succeeded. The 6 threads noise.0 through noise.5 were all active within the same ~300 ms stretch, so many model calls were issued in a tight burst. [from probe_self_diagnose, probe_self_explain_turn]
3. Each failed work_step failed on attempt 1 with duration_ms 0-4. Sub-millisecond rejections rule out network timeouts or upstream slowness; this is a local rate limiter refusing calls instantly once the burst budget was spent, which is why the code is rate_limited rather than a timeout or transport error. [from probe_self_explain_turn]
4. Impact was limited: 30 of 38 effects succeeded and all 6 requests completed; thread.noise.5's execution checkpointed running then completed despite the 8 failed work_step effects, so the failures degraded that turn's work rather than taking the runtime down. [from probe_self_timeline]
5. Codes considered and excluded: there are no timeout, connection, unauthorized, validation, or approval-denied codes in the window; rate_limited is the sole failure code and the only one that explains both the burst timing and the near-zero failure latencies. [from probe_self_timeline, probe_self_diagnose]
Still unknown:
- Full per-rule fired-rule detail and per-operation latency breakdown from probe_self_diagnose: The diagnose artifact is a single long JSON line that recall_output only exposes truncated, so I could not read the operations array or any rule list beyond the aggregate counters (effects failed:8, succeeded:30).
- The rate limiter's configuration (burst size, refill rate, per-model vs global scope): The workspace contains no source or config files, so the threshold that the burst of model calls tripped cannot be confirmed from the record.
- Retry/backoff policy outcome for the 8 failed work_step effects: Each effect shows only attempt 1 failed with no retry recorded, so it is unknown whether retries were configured, exhausted, or suppressed by the turn completing.
Proposed next actions (not executed; ask for one to run it through approval):
1. Raise or re-tune the model-call rate limiter's burst/refill budget, or add jittered backoff and retry for Tamoz::Agent::ModelCallError code rate_limited on model.converse.work_step.: The burst pattern (6 concurrent threads issuing plan and work_step calls milliseconds apart, instant 0-4 ms rejections) points at a local limiter with a budget too small for concurrent turns, not an upstream outage. [from probe_self_explain_turn, probe_self_diagnose]
2. Add a configured check that alerts when effect attempts with code rate_limited exceed a small threshold per window.: Today the window shows degraded:false even though 8 of 38 effects failed; a threshold-based check would surface this degradation automatically. [from probe_self_timeline]

findings.statement: Every ponds MCP call in the window failed with the same single error code: Tamoz::MCP::TransportError / transport_timeout. Three tool.mcp.ponds.query attempts failed cleanly and one tool.mcp.ponds.set_aerator attempt ended with unknown outcome, all in thread.noise.5 around 1791144421170-1791144421188.

The failures are isolated to the ponds MCP dependency. In the same window the runtime core was healthy: all 6 turns requested/completed, all 6 approval asks were approved, model.generate.plan went 18/18 and tool.read_file 12/12 with p95 of 0-6ms.

The critical consequence is not the failed reads but the set_aerator effect: its outcome is unknown (rule effect.outcome_unknown, severity critical), so an external state change may or may not have happened and the record says it is waiting for a human to reconcile, never to blind-retry. The three query failures were plain failed status (rule effect.repeated_failure, category dependency_unavailable).

transport_timeout is the only error code present in the whole window's record, on both fired rules and all four evidence attempts. There is no competing code (no auth, not_found, or rejected-request codes), so the repeated-failure rule and the unknown-outcome rule share one underlying cause rather than two.

Attempts failed in 0-1ms each, i.e. instant transport errors rather than waits hitting a deadline, and none were retried (attempt 1 only). This is consistent with the ponds MCP server transport being immediately unreachable, and the failed queries show the thread had already lost that dependency before the mutating call was attempted.

gaps.datum: Server-side state of the ponds MCP server at failure time (process down, socket refused, or hung listener)
gaps.why: The probes only record the client-side transport errors; the server's own logs are outside this record, so 'unreachable' is inferred from instant TransportErrors, not observed directly.

gaps.datum: Whether the set_aerator change actually took effect on the external pond system
gaps.why: The effect status is unknown by definition; only checking the external system and settling with tamoz resolve can determine it.

proposals.action: Check the ponds MCP server and its transport (process, socket/endpoint) and restore it before any MCP call is retried.
proposals.rationale: All four failures share one code, transport_timeout, and the repeated-failure rule says to fix the single cause instead of retrying calls against a dead dependency.

proposals.action: Manually verify the pond aerator state on the external system, then settle the unknown effect (key sha256:052051af..., execution 836b1ad8-fdf5-49a1-9c43-03a4fc372a61) with tamoz resolve; do not blind-retry it.

All MCP calls to the ponds server failed with Tamoz::MCP::TransportError code transport_timeout: three tool.mcp.ponds.query calls failed and one tool.mcp.ponds.set_aerator call was left with an unknown outcome, all in thread.noise.5. Everything else in the window (6 turns, approvals, plan generation, read_file) succeeded, so the failure is confined to the ponds MCP dependency.
Hypothesis (high confidence): transport_timeout
Findings:
1. Every ponds MCP call in the window failed with the same single error code: Tamoz::MCP::TransportError / transport_timeout. Three tool.mcp.ponds.query attempts failed cleanly and one tool.mcp.ponds.set_aerator attempt ended with unknown outcome, all in thread.noise.5 around 1791144421170-1791144421188. [from probe_self_diagnose, probe_self_explain_turn, probe_self_timeline]
2. The failures are isolated to the ponds MCP dependency. In the same window the runtime core was healthy: all 6 turns requested/completed, all 6 approval asks were approved, model.generate.plan went 18/18 and tool.read_file 12/12 with p95 of 0-6ms. [from probe_self_timeline, probe_self_explain_turn]
3. The critical consequence is not the failed reads but the set_aerator effect: its outcome is unknown (rule effect.outcome_unknown, severity critical), so an external state change may or may not have happened and the record says it is waiting for a human to reconcile, never to blind-retry. The three query failures were plain failed status (rule effect.repeated_failure, category dependency_unavailable). [from probe_self_diagnose, probe_self_explain_turn]
4. transport_timeout is the only error code present in the whole window's record, on both fired rules and all four evidence attempts. There is no competing code (no auth, not_found, or rejected-request codes), so the repeated-failure rule and the unknown-outcome rule share one underlying cause rather than two. [from probe_self_diagnose]
5. Attempts failed in 0-1ms each, i.e. instant transport errors rather than waits hitting a deadline, and none were retried (attempt 1 only). This is consistent with the ponds MCP server transport being immediately unreachable, and the failed queries show the thread had already lost that dependency before the mutating call was attempted. [from probe_self_explain_turn]
Still unknown:
- Server-side state of the ponds MCP server at failure time (process down, socket refused, or hung listener): The probes only record the client-side transport errors; the server's own logs are outside this record, so 'unreachable' is inferred from instant TransportErrors, not observed directly.
- Whether the set_aerator change actually took effect on the external pond system: The effect status is unknown by definition; only checking the external system and settling with tamoz resolve can determine it.
Proposed next actions (not executed; ask for one to run it through approval):
1. Check the ponds MCP server and its transport (process, socket/endpoint) and restore it before any MCP call is retried.: All four failures share one code, transport_timeout, and the repeated-failure rule says to fix the single cause instead of retrying calls against a dead dependency. [from probe_self_diagnose, probe_self_timeline]
2. Manually verify the pond aerator state on the external system, then settle the unknown effect (key sha256:052051af..., execution 836b1ad8-fdf5-49a1-9c43-03a4fc372a61) with tamoz resolve; do not blind-retry it.: The effect.outcome_unknown rule marks this as critical and waiting for a human: the aerator may already be on or off, so the external state must be checked before reconciling. [from probe_self_diagnose]

findings.statement: In the 240-minute window there were 6 completed turns (thread.noise.0 through thread.noise.5) and 36 effect attempts: 30 succeeded, 6 failed. All 6 failures are model calls, all inside thread.noise.5, and all at 1791144807306-1791144807319, i.e. within about 13 ms of each other.

5 of the 6 failures are model.generate.plan attempts, each a distinct effect (effect keys sha256:ded4..., 341e..., 3288..., 4b96..., 84b9...), each failing on attempt 1 with Tamoz::Agent::ModelCallError code authentication_failed. The repeated-failure rule (effect.repeated_failure, severity high) and the model.call_failed rule both fired only on this class/code pair.

Within the same execution (c9ffd632..., thread.noise.5), three earlier model.generate.plan calls (created 07285-07294) and two tool.read_file calls succeeded; the credential then started being refused from 07306 onward. The failure is mid-turn onset, not a dead runtime: read_file (a local tool) kept working right up to 07304, and only provider-bound model calls began failing.

The 6th failure is a single model.generate.review attempt with code rate_limited at 07319, after the 5 authentication_failed failures. It is one occurrence, did not repeat, and no rule fired on it as a repeated failure. If rate limiting were the root cause you would expect it first and repeatedly; instead authentication_failed starts first and dominates 5:1.

The failing calls were never retried (attempt 1 only on every failed effect) and the turn still completed, with diagnose reporting degraded=false. So the damage is the lost plan/review work for thread.noise.5, not a hung or broken turn loop; the write_file approvals for noise.1-5 all asked and were approved normally.

The diagnose action text notes that a refused key, an empty account or a rate limit is a provider problem, not a Tamoz bug. The evidence agrees: no worker errors were logged, effects and checkpoints are consistent, and the failure pattern is credential refusal from a provider mid-turn.

gaps.datum: Provider-side detail for the refusals (HTTP status, account/key id, raw provider message) behind the authentication_failed code.
gaps.why: The probes record only class and code; whether the key was rotated, revoked, or exhausted mid-turn cannot be distinguished from the record.

gaps.datum: Which model provider/endpoint each failed call targeted (plan vs review).
gaps.why: It would confirm whether the single rate_limited review call used a different key than the failing plan key, or shared the same quota.

gaps.datum: Whether any retry/backoff policy was configured for ModelCallError.
gaps.why: All 6 failed effects show exactly one attempt; I cannot tell from the record whether retry was suppressed by policy or by the error class.

proposals.action: Rotate or repair the model provider API key used by this runtime, then replay the failed work for thread.noise.5 (5 plan generations and 1 review).
proposals.rationale: 5 repeated authentication_failed refusals starting mid-turn at 1791144807306 indicate the credential became invalid or its account drained while earlier calls with the same configuration succeeded.

proposals.action: Add an alert or circuit-breaker on ModelCallError/authentication_failed so credential loss is surfaced after the first occurrence instead of being burned through on 5 consecutive calls.
proposals.rationale: The repeated-failure rule did fire, but only after 5 identical failures within 11 ms; fail-fast on a non-retryable auth error would stop the burst and make the incident cheaper to notice.

proposals.action: Treat rate_limited on the review call as secondary; re-check it after the key is fixed and only escalate if it recurs.
proposals.rationale: It is a single occurrence after the auth failures, consistent with collateral backoff/quota pressure rather than an independent root cause.

A real dependency outage would show network-class errors and retries; a sub-millisecond refusal means the egress gate rejected the destination before any network call was made.

It is not one poisoned effect being retried: the four failures have four distinct effect keys and task ids, all inside thread.noise.5. findings.statement: The runtime is flagged degraded with exactly one reason: 'the telemetry journal counted 240 dropped signals' (240 drops in both the 4h and 24h windows, so all the loss is recent).

Summary: Investigated the degraded Tamoz runtime over the last 4 and 24 hours using its own record. The only problem the record contains is telemetry journal loss: 240 tamoz.model.call signals were dropped because the journal queue was full (error class queue_full), which is what set the degraded flag. The durable path was entirely healthy — 6/6 turns completed, 30/30 effects succeeded, zero failed or unknown attempts, zero logged worker errors — so no user-visible work failed.
Hypothesis (high confidence): queue_full
Findings:
1. The runtime is flagged degraded with exactly one reason: 'the telemetry journal counted 240 dropped signals' (240 drops in both the 4h and 24h windows, so all the loss is recent). [from probe_self_diagnose]
2. The single fired rule is telemetry.loss (severity low, category resource_exhausted) with detail drops = {tamoz.model.call:queue_full:bulk: 240}: 240 telemetry signals of kind tamoz.model.call were bulk-dropped with error class queue_full, i.e. the journal queue filled. first_seen_ms and last_seen_ms are null, so drop timestamps are not recorded. [from probe_self_diagnose]
3. The durable record shows no other failure anywhere: 6/6 requests completed, 30/30 effects succeeded, 0 failed and 0 unknown attempts, occurrences (worker error log) is 0, and the timeline has no threads with failures. [from probe_self_diagnose]
4. The event timeline in the window contains only successful events (turns requested and completed, write_file approvals asked and approved) and no failed or unknown effects. [from probe_self_timeline]
5. A sampled thread's decision record (thread.noise.3) confirms clean execution: the execution completed, all 5 effects (3x model.generate.plan, 2x tool.read_file) succeeded on attempt 1, and approval decision.21e5de10 was approved. [from probe_self_explain_turn]
6. Alternative codes considered and rejected: 'telemetry.loss' is the rule_id of the fired rule, not an error code; 'tamoz.model.call' is the signal kind that was dropped, not the error; 'bulk' is the drop mode; 'resource_exhausted' is the finding's category label and fits the situation but is a classification, not the specific error code — the error class carried by each dropped signal is queue_full. [from probe_self_diagnose]
Still unknown:
- Disk space and journal directory state: The probes cannot observe the filesystem; the fired rule's action says to check disk space and the journal directory, so the physical trigger of the queue_full condition is inferred, not confirmed.
- Drop timestamps: first_seen_ms and last_seen_ms are null in the finding, so the moment the queue filled within the window cannot be pinned.
- Semantics of the ':bulk' suffix: The probe output does not document whether 'bulk' is a drop mode or a drop reason; it does not change the error class but limits precision about the drop mechanism.
- Journal consumer identity and drain rate: No probe exposes who consumes the journal or why it fell behind, so slow consumer vs full disk cannot be distinguished.
Proposed next actions (not executed; ask for one to run it through approval):
1. Check disk space and the journal directory's capacity and retention on the host running this runtime.: The fired rule's own remediation says the durable record is unaffected but counts from the journal are lower bounds and the queue filled (queue_full, resource_exhausted); a full or slow journal directory is the likely physical trigger. [from probe_self_diagnose]
2. Raise the journal queue bound or add an earlier alert before bulk drops occur, and record drop timestamps instead of null first_seen/last_seen.: 240 signals were silently bulk-dropped with no timestamps; earlier warning and timestamped drops would make the onset diagnosable from the record alone. [from probe_self_diagnose]

The dominant failure is 8 consecutive tool.read_file calls failing with Tamoz::Agent::ToolError / not_found between 1791145013332 and 1791145013349, each on attempt 1 with no retry. The rule effect.repeated_failure (severity high, category dependency_unavailable) fired on exactly this pattern (rule finding sha256:d92315059838f5a307ed74b9e262657ebdc3b3a9eb81b9ec80409b9e84f7f07a).

The read tool itself works: two tool.read_file calls in the same turn immediately before the failures succeeded (1791145013327, 1791145013329). So the 8 not_found failures are about specific missing paths, not a broken read tool.

After the 8 failed reads, the same turn issued tool.mcp.ponds.set_aerator, whose single attempt ended unknown with Tamoz::MCP::TransportError / transport_timeout at 1791145013353. The rule effect.outcome_unknown (severity critical) fired: the effect needs reconciliation against the external system and is waiting for a human (rule finding sha256:9925624e4993041478102ddb2b2e988f928e42c33701cb5f3c98690c0813c1cd).

Everything else in the window is healthy: 6 requests completed, 30 of 39 effects succeeded, model.generate.plan succeeded on all 18 attempts (16 of them inside the failing turn), and latency p95 is ~1ms. No logged worker errors beyond the effect failures, and the degraded flag is false.

Alternative codes considered and rejected as root cause: transport_timeout (one event, later in time, describes an unresolved outcome of a downstream call rather than a cause - though it is the most operationally urgent item since the aerator state is unknown); dependency_unavailable is the category of the rule attached to not_found, i.e. expected input files were absent.
